<div class="project-content">

<p class="lede-para">
  Roughly one in ten American adults lives with diabetes, and a large share of them are undiagnosed. This project asks a
  narrow, tractable version of that problem: given routine clinical measurements, how accurately can we flag someone as
  high-risk — and which measurements are actually doing the work?
</p>

<div class="results">
  <div class="result"><span class="num">97%</span><span class="lbl">Test-set accuracy</span></div>
  <div class="result"><span class="num">0.99</span><span class="lbl">ROC-AUC</span></div>
  <div class="result"><span class="num">9,538</span><span class="lbl">Patient records</span></div>
  <div class="result"><span class="num">4</span><span class="lbl">Final predictors</span></div>
</div>

<h2>Data and preprocessing</h2>

<p>
  The dataset holds 9,538 medical records with demographic, lifestyle and biometric fields. It arrived unusually clean —
  no missing values and no outliers worth removing — so preprocessing focused on the relationships between variables
  rather than repair work.
</p>

<ul>
  <li>Checked multicollinearity with <strong>Variance Inflation Factor</strong>, which flagged fasting glucose and HbA1c
  as strongly correlated. Glucose was dropped: HbA1c carries a longer-horizon signal and is the more clinically stable
  of the two.</li>
  <li>Standardized numeric predictors and encoded categorical fields with the Tidyverse.</li>
</ul>

<h2>Feature selection</h2>

<ul>
  <li>Ran <strong>stepwise regression</strong> to narrow the predictor set.</li>
  <li>Settled on four variables: <strong>age, BMI, HbA1c, and family history</strong>.</li>
  <li>Confirmed with <strong>ANOVA</strong> that the reduced model performed comparably to the full model — the extra
  predictors were not earning their complexity.</li>
</ul>

<h2>Modeling and evaluation</h2>

<ul>
  <li>Fit <strong>logistic regression</strong> as the primary classifier on a 70/30 train-test split.</li>
  <li>Confusion matrix on held-out data: <strong>97% accuracy</strong>, with high recall on positive cases — the metric
  that matters most for a screening tool, where a missed case costs more than a false alarm.</li>
  <li><strong>5-fold cross-validation</strong> returned RMSE 0.146, R² 0.906 and MAE 0.04, indicating the fit was stable
  rather than a lucky split.</li>
  <li>The ROC curve yielded an <strong>AUC of 0.99</strong>.</li>
</ul>

<h2>What the model says</h2>

<ul>
  <li><strong>HbA1c, BMI and age</strong> are the dominant predictors, with family history acting as a modifier rather
  than a driver on its own.</li>
  <li>Examining family history across age bands showed the effect concentrating in older cohorts.</li>
  <li>The BMI × HbA1c interaction is where risk compounds: elevated metabolic indicators together shift diagnosis
  likelihood far more than either does alone.</li>
  <li>Practically, this argues for monitoring metabolic health early rather than screening on age alone.</li>
</ul>

<h2>Limitations</h2>

<ul>
  <li>The dataset carries no diet, exercise, or socioeconomic variables — all of which are known confounders.</li>
  <li>Measurement practices vary across clinical sites, which introduces noise the model can't see.</li>
  <li>97% accuracy on a clean secondary dataset is not 97% accuracy in a clinic. This is a modeling exercise, not a
  diagnostic tool.</li>
  <li>Next steps I'd take: gender-specific risk profiles, BMI × gender interactions, and validation on an external
  cohort.</li>
</ul>
